title: Aida
facts: Aida was commissioned by Cairo’s Khedivial Opera House and premiered there on 24 December 1871.
The premiere was delayed because the sets and costumes were stuck in Paris during the Prussian siege of 1870–71.
Verdi didn’t go to Cairo. He disliked that the audience was all invited dignitaries and critics, and counted the 1872 La Scala opening as the real premiere.
Verdi wrote a full overture to replace this short prelude, then dropped it for its “pretentious silliness” (his own words).
Verdi’s rejected Aida overture got a rare broadcast in 1940 from Toscanini and the NBC Symphony, but was never released commercially.
Verdi agreed to write Aida, on a story idea by the Egyptologist Auguste Mariette, for 150,000 francs.
Auguste Mariette designed the costumes for the Cairo premiere; the sets were painted in Paris by the Opéra’s scene painters.
Verdi wrote the role of Aida for Teresa Stolz, who first sang it at the Milan premiere.
Amneris|Fu la sorte|Ohimè! morir mi sento|L.abborrita rivale
Maria Waldmann, the Milan Amneris, was Verdi’s favourite in the role; she sang it many times at his request.
In Rio de Janeiro in 1886, after the conductor and two replacements failed, a 19-year-old cellist named Arturo Toscanini conducted Aida from memory, with great success.
At the Met alone, Aida has been sung more than 1,100 times since 1886.
Aida reached the Met on 12 November 1886, conducted by Anton Seidl.
The King names Radamès commander, and the court erupts: “Su! del Nilo al sacro lido”, then “Guerra, guerra, guerra!”
Solemn ceremonies and priestesses’ dances in the temple: “Possente Ptah”.
